messages.subject: Using Distance R package to estimate density of gibbons - point transect with cue count multiplier.
messages.subject_clean: Using Distance R package to estimate density of gibbons - point transect with cue count multiplier.
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm a Masters student and I am using the Distance R package for part of my dissertation project. I am trying to estimate gibbon density from point transect survey data. The survey consisted of six arrays of three listening posts distributed throughout one forest strata (pristine). Each array was surveyed for four days and surveyors estimated the distance to calling groups from their posts. I want to calculate the estimated group density of the gibbons using distance. I have a couple of questions about using the R package that I thought people here may be able to help with:

1. Most papers I have read which used distance sampling for analysing gibbon point transect data have measured from a single average point for each array (set of three listening posts) and an average location for each detected gibbon group. However, I have recently read a paper (DOI: 10.1002/ajp.23169) in which the researchers measured the distance from each individual listening post in an array to each detected group. Which method would people recommend for this kind of analysis?

2. As I want to estimate the group density, I have grouped the survey data in GIS using triangulation and the call times. For example, group 1 consists of three detections (three distance estimates) made by each of the three listening posts in array 1. How can I include this in my input data for the R package? Can I just put a column for "cluster" in my distance input csv to specify that there is more than one distance recorded for most groups?

3. I have calculated the effective sampling area of my arrays in GIS prior to the distance analysis. Each array has a different effective sampling area. Can I still run distance analysis for all the arrays at the same time? Or would I have to the analysis separately for each array?

4. Do I need to specify which listening post in each array detected each group? (e.g. listening post 1 detected groups 1, 3 and 6).

5. For the survey data, I need to adjust the density estimate by the estimate of calling probability in one day. I'm a bit confused as to how I should use the dht2 function for this. I am using an Excel package to estimate the calling probability in one day of the gibbons from the survey data. The estimate gives my calling probability and it's variance. Can I just enter the calling probability as a cue rate column into my distance input file (e.g. for my data the calling probability in one day is estimated to be 0.7, so can I just put 0.7 cue rate for all the detections?)

Many thanks,
Toby

messages.body_plain:
Toby

I don't claim to be an expert in analysis of gibbon acoustic detection data, but here are my thoughts on your questions.

1. My understanding is that an array will give rise to a single detection distance, measured from the centre of the array.  The reason for the multiple listening posts is to perform the triangulation to determine the location of the vocalisation.  With that location determined, the distance from the vocalisation to the centre of the array is the radial distance that will be analysed.

2. Each detection by an array is a single detection, not three records for a group detection.

3. I presume you wish to make inference to the forest stratum in which the arrays were located.  Therefore information from all arrays are analysed together.  Effective sampling area is computed across all arrays.  The exception would be if there were array-specific covariates involved in the analysis.

4. No

5. The estimated calling rate and its precision are called "multipliers".  Have a look at the vignette regarding cue count surveys (your gibbon survey) at our Examples website (http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-cues/cuecounts-distill.html).  In the section about `dht2` you will see how to create a named list "mult" that contains the call rate and its standard error.  The list "mult" is passed as the argument "multipliers" to the `dht2` function.  This converts density of calls to density of groups.

Hope that answers some of your questions.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Eric,

Thanks very much for the quick reply and the detailed answers. I've worked through the cue count survey vignette, which was incredibly helpful. However, I still have some questions regarding the specifics of my data analysis that maybe you can help me with:

In the vignette, it states that for cue count you need to specify search time rather than effort. For my data, each array was surveyed for four days (each day between the hours of an average of 4 am - 8 am) and the cue rate I'm using is calling probability on one day (the probability that gibbons will call on one day). In the guidance, it states that the unit of search time and the unit of the cue rate have to be the same. The cue rate is based one day, so should I do 24 hours for the cue rate and 4 hours for search time? Or should I say that the cue rate was one day and the search time was 4 days? Or does it not matter as either option gives a search time of 4? Additionally, do you need to tell the package what units both cue rate and search time is in e.g. days or hours?

For the cue.rate.se <http://cue.rate.se> command, does the value have to be the standard error? As I mentioned previously, the method I am using to calculate calling probability in one day gives the variance not standard error. Could I use this variance value instead of standard error for the cue.rate.se <http://cue.rate.se>?

If I want to estimate the effective detection radius in the R package using a maximum listening distance of 1000 m, how would I do that? I calculated an Effective Listening Area of each array for the Triangulation analysis, which I have input into the area column in my input csv for the R package, but I've seen some papers that calculate Effective Detection Radius in Distance and I was unsure whether this would be more accurate.

Do you think I should I only include groups which bearing estimates triangulate? In addition to Distance Sampling, I’m also analysing the survey data using acoustic spatial capture-recapture (ASCR). That does not require for bearing estimates to triangulate as it factors in bearing error. Can Distance do a similar thing?

·Some of the arrays are within a few hundred meters away from a different stratum that I do not want to estimate the density for (in my case I only want to estimate the density in the pristine forest area but there are two other strata in the study site: once-burnt and twice-burnt). For the triangulation analysis, I used ArcMap clip each array ELA to the pristine forest polygon to ensure that none of the ELA included burnt forest. I then only included triangulated points that fell within the ELA. Should I do the same for distance? Or would the omission of data lead to bias? Would a better option be to input a raster which is classified as pristine forest = 1, once-burnt/twice burnt = 0, so that I can tell the software the extent of the pristine forest and which points fall outside it?
Many thanks,
Toby

messages.body_plain:
Toby

Further thoughts, my bullets correspond to your bullets--
Hopefully you can convert the call probability of 0.7 in a day into a rate.  Would it make sense that there were 0.7 calls in 4 hours of listening?  That could be converted to an hourly call rate of 0.175 calls per hour, eh?  You would need to adjust your measure of precision as well.
Yes, the value required does need to be a standard error, not a variance.
Effective detection radius is maximum listening distance divided by detection probability (provided in `ds()` output).
`ds()` cannot incorporate uncertainty in bearings in the analysis
I think you are describing the potential of making detections outside your "study area", in this case your pristine habitat type.  You could impose more stringent truncation of your radial distances (eliminating the most distant detections); this would be another way to solve this problem.

What you mentioned about the cue rates makes sense. I will try and figure out another way of calculating calling probability in one day so that I can generate a standard error.

I have a couple of quick questions:
I just did a test run of the cue count analysis using the data from two of the six arrays in my data. When I tried to run the ds function, I got an error message stating that the region areas are not consistent. This is true, as the two arrays I inputted in my csv file have different values in the area column because they have different estimates of effective listening areas that I have estimated in GIS. Each array that I am analysing has a different estimated effective listening area. How do I get around this error and analyse all the data from all six arrays together?
If I included two detections that I have grouped together based on their call times and proximity to each other but which the bearings do not triangulate, would that violate some of the Distance Sampling assumptions (e.g. measurements are exact)?
Many thanks,
Toby

The "area" you should specify is the size of your pristine forest to which you wish to make inference; it is nothing to do with the listening areas of each array.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Eric,

Sorry, I have one further question:

The paper I mentioned previously (Vu et al. 2018) and another paper by those authors calculated gibbon density in Distance using a slightly different method. They suggested that the assumption that g0 =1 will not be met as by using the average location of groups, the smallest distances near the listening post may be missed due to location average stepping. Furthermore, they suggest that as gibbons do not sing every day,  the assumption of g0=1 at the point can not be assumed to be true for all four survey days. They addressed this problem by doing a point transect analysis and setting g0 to equal the calling probability in one day (which for my case would be 0.7) to adjust the density estimate. What are your thoughts on this? Do you think this is a good approach or is it better to follow the cue count method and adjust the estimate using the cue rate?

Many thanks,
Toby

messages.subject: Convergence failure in MCDS
messages.subject_clean: Convergence failure in MCDS
messages.body_plain:
Dear All:
I am fitting a half-normal key function with a single factor covariate using the MCDS analysis engine in Distance 7.3.  Convergence was not achieved, but the outcome resulted in the most parsimonious of the models I've tested.  I tried to achieve convergence by setting starting values for the three parameters in the model, but to no avail.

Regarding this, my question is, should I ignore the failure to converge and use the results obtained from fitting this model, or should I reject this model in favour of another (the second best option) which does converge?

Thanks and regards,
Stuart Cairns

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Convergence failure in MCDS
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Convergence failure in MCDS
messages.body_plain:
Stuart

When software fails to converge, this means the parameter estimates produced are not the maximum likelihood estimates, nor is the reported likelihood (and associated AIC value) the maximum likelihood.

If contrasting the AIC score of a model that did not converge with the AIC score of a model that did converge, you would not be comparing like with like.  Therefore I would suggest not using the results from the model that did not converge.  You would also want to investigate symptoms in the data the could result in models that do not converge.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Eric,

I have some further questions regarding the method of analysing gibbon data using the Distance R package.

1. I'm comparing estimates produced by triangulation, Acoustic Spatial Capture-recapture (ASCR) and Distance. I asked Ben Stevenson, the person who created the ASCR R package, about whether I can compare estimates produced by using cue rate with those produced by ASCR. He said that the calling probability in one day is a just saying that we expect 70% of groups to call in one day, it says nothing about how often they are calling. Therefore, it is not possible to convert from the probability of calls to calls emitted per hour as they are different things. I am adjusting the ASCR result using the calling probability in one day, therefore, I guess I need to take the other approach (i.e. fixing g0 to equal the calling probability in one day, e.g. 0.7) even though it's more unorthodox.

2. The paper I mentioned before measured the distance from each listening post in an array to each group detected for each of the four survey days. They said that if you only measure from a central point of listening posts to the central point of a detected group "the smallest distances recorded might be missed due to the “location averaging step” and lead to the violation of the assumption of perfect detection near the listening posts (g(0) = 1)". They, therefore, took this approach: "We measured
the distance from a listening post to the locations of a gibbon group every day and divulged the “effort” for repeated surveys in a Distance data file. In our case, if a gibbon group was detected from a listening post on n > 1 days, there would be n observations used in the analysis. Similarly, if a gibbon group was detected from m> 1 listening posts in the same day, there would be m observations used in the analysis. This did not bias the estimate of gibbon group density because m listening posts were declared in the data file. As we treated each day as one survey effort, the detection probability near the listening post was <1.0 because gibbons do not call every day. Therefore, we set the detection probability near the listening post g(0) to equal gibbon calling probability."

I think that they considered each one of the three posts in an array as a point transect rather than the whole array (the central point of the three listening posts) to be the point transect.

 Do you have any thoughts on this approach? I know that you are not a gibbon expert, but I just wanted to ask your thoughts on this from a Distance Sampling expert perspective.

Many thanks,
Toby

messages.body_plain:
Toby, briefly, yes, Ben is right that the cue rate  for the cue count method is not the same as the proportion of groups that call in a day.  The difference arises because a group may call more than once on a given day.  On your second question, I’m probably mis-understanding the method.  I think using each listening post as a point is an acceptable approach, but then the effort on a given day should be the number of listening posts, regardless of whether any groups were heard from those posts.  And for each group detected, you would need to estimate its distance from each listening post that detected it.  So a single group, detected from more than one listening post, would contribute a detection distance to more than one point.

Steve Buckland

From: distance...@googlegroups.com [mailto:distance...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of Toby Pilkington

To: distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Using Distance R package to estimate density of gibbons - point transect with cue count multiplier.

Hi Eric,

I have some further questions regarding the method of analysing gibbon data using the Distance R package.

1. I'm comparing estimates produced by triangulation, Acoustic Spatial Capture-recapture (ASCR) and Distance. I asked Ben Stevenson, the person who created the ASCR R package, about whether I can compare estimates produced by using cue rate with those produced by ASCR. He said that the calling probability in one day is a just saying that we expect 70% of groups to call in one day, it says nothing about how often they are calling. Therefore, it is not possible to convert from the probability of calls to calls emitted per hour as they are different things. I am adjusting the ASCR result using the calling probability in one day, therefore, I guess I need to take the other approach (i.e. fixing g0 to equal the calling probability in one day, e.g. 0.7) even though it's more unorthodox.

2. The paper I mentioned before measured the distance from each listening post in an array to each group detected for each of the four survey days. They said that if you only measure from a central point of listening posts to the central point of a detected group "the smallest distances recorded might be missed due to the “location averaging step” and lead to the violation of the assumption of perfect detection near the listening posts (g(0) = 1)". They, therefore, took this approach: "We measured

the distance from a listening post to the locations of a gibbon group every day and divulged the “effort” for repeated surveys in a Distance data file. In our case, if a gibbon group was detected from a listening post on n > 1 days, there would be n observations used in the analysis. Similarly, if a gibbon group was detected from m> 1 listening posts in the same day, there would be m observations used in the analysis. This did not bias the estimate of gibbon group density because m listening posts were declared in the data file. As we treated each day as one survey effort, the detection probability near the listening post was <1.0 because gibbons do not call every day. Therefore, we set the detection probability near the listening post g(0) to equal gibbon calling probability."

I think that they considered each one of the three posts in an array as a point transect rather than the whole array (the central point of the three listening posts) to be the point transect.

 Do you have any thoughts on this approach? I know that you are not a gibbon expert, but I just wanted to ask your thoughts on this from a Distance Sampling expert perspective.

Many thanks,

Toby

messages.body_plain:
Hi Toby,

If I understand you correctly, I think you have a problem if you set g(0) to equal the probability of an individual gibbon (or gibbon group) calling per day. This is because whether a gibbon calls during any time in the day is far less relevant then whether it calls whenever it is at 0 distance. Imagine that an individual gibbon (or group) calls every day (so probability of calling per day is 1), but only calls for 10% of the time while at 0 distance. This would make probability of detection at 0 distance 10%.

What I think you need is the probability that a gibbon (or group) calls during each period/snapshot that you work out a density for. If your snapshots are more or less instantaneous (which would conform to classic distance sampling assumptions) then this probability is (more or less) equal to the proportion of time that gibbons spend calling (assuming calls are randomly distributed over the course of the day). If you are working on a period basis, you would have to calculate/estimate the probability of calling within that period.

Hope that makes sense!

Mark

On Friday, 11 September 2020 at 11:19:12 UTC+1 Stephen Buckland wrote:
>
> Toby, briefly, yes, Ben is right that the cue rate  for the cue count method is not the same as the proportion of groups that call in a day.  The difference arises because a group may call more than once on a given day.  On your second question, I’m probably mis-understanding the method.  I think using each listening post as a point is an acceptable approach, but then the effort on a given day should be the number of listening posts, regardless of whether any groups were heard from those posts.  And for each group detected, you would need to estimate its distance from each listening post that detected it.  So a single group, detected from more than one listening post, would contribute a detection distance to more than one point.

I asked Ben Stevenson, the person who created the ASCR R package, about whether I can compare estimates produced by using cue rate with those produced by ASCR. He said that the calling probability in one day is a just saying that we expect 70% of groups to call in one day, it says nothing about how often they are calling. Therefore, it is not possible to convert from the probability of calls to calls emitted per hour as they are different things. I am adjusting the ASCR result using the calling probability in one day, therefore, I guess I need to take the other approach (i.e. fixing g0 to equal the calling probability in one day, e.g. 0.7) even though it's more unorthodox.
>
>
>
> 2. The paper I mentioned before measured the distance from each listening post in an array to each group detected for each of the four survey days. They said that if you only measure from a central point of listening posts to the central point of a detected group "the smallest distances recorded might be missed due to the “location averaging step” and lead to the violation of the assumption of perfect detection near the listening posts (g(0) = 1)". They, therefore, took this approach: "We measured
>
> the distance from a listening post to the locations of a gibbon group every day and divulged the “effort” for repeated surveys in a Distance data file. In our case, if a gibbon group was detected from a listening post on n > 1 days, there would be n observations used in the analysis. Similarly, if a gibbon group was detected from m> 1 listening posts in the same day, there would be m observations used in the analysis. This did not bias the estimate of gibbon group density because m listening posts were declared in the data file. As we treated each day as one survey effort, the detection probability near the listening post was <1.0 because gibbons do not call every day. Therefore, we set the detection probability near the listening post g(0) to equal gibbon calling probability."
>
>
>
> I think that they considered each one of the three posts in an array as a point transect rather than the whole array (the central point of the three listening posts) to be the point transect.
>
>
>
>  Do you have any thoughts on this approach? I know that you are not a gibbon expert, but I just wanted to ask your thoughts on this from a Distance Sampling expert perspective.

>
>
> Many thanks,

Which method would people recommend for this kind of analysis?
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > 2. As I want to estimate the group density, I have grouped the survey data in GIS using triangulation and the call times. For example, group 1 consists of three detections (three distance estimates) made by each of the three listening posts in array 1. How can I include this in my input data for the R package? Can I just put a column for "cluster" in my distance input csv to specify that there is more than one distance recorded for most groups?
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > 3. I have calculated the effective sampling area of my arrays in GIS prior to the distance analysis. Each array has a different effective sampling area. Can I still run distance analysis for all the arrays at the same time? Or would I have to the analysis separately for each array?
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > 4. Do I need to specify which listening post in each array detected each group? (e.g. listening post 1 detected groups 1, 3 and 6).
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > 5. For the survey data, I need to adjust the density estimate by the estimate of calling probability in one day. I'm a bit confused as to how I should use the dht2 function for this. I am using an Excel package to estimate the calling probability in one day of the gibbons from the survey data. The estimate gives my calling probability and it's variance. Can I just enter the calling probability as a cue rate column into my distance input file (e.g. for my data the calling probability in one day is estimated to be 0.7, so can I just put 0.7 cue rate for all the detections?)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Many thanks,

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark,

Thanks very much for the information. Each array was surveyed for a rough average of four hours per day (8 am -11 am). The calling probability I have estimated is based on data collected within these four hours, not really one day, just one survey day. I guess that means it's the period method? I'm sorry, I'm not familiar with all the terminology. This calling probability I am using is generated from a gibbon density Excel package that uses the survey data to estimate it. I am using the calling probability in one day produced by this package for both the triangulation analysis and the ASCR, so I think I need to use the same one for distance.

Also, regarding the g(0), I don't really understand why the researchers set g(0) to equal the calling probability. Surely in the field, a gibbon would be detected if it was singing above the point transect that you were based at.

So, would it be correct to run the analysis using g(0) =1 and then adjust the density estimate produced by the calling probability in one day using the dht2 function?

Thanks,
Toby

On Friday, 11 September 2020 at 11:35:19 UTC+1 Mark Wilson wrote:
> Hi Toby,
>
> If I understand you correctly, I think you have a problem if you set g(0) to equal the probability of an individual gibbon (or gibbon group) calling per day. This is because whether a gibbon calls during any time in the day is far less relevant then whether it calls whenever it is at 0 distance. Imagine that an individual gibbon (or group) calls every day (so probability of calling per day is 1), but only calls for 10% of the time while at 0 distance. This would make probability of detection at 0 distance 10%.
>
> What I think you need is the probability that a gibbon (or group) calls during each period/snapshot that you work out a density for. If your snapshots are more or less instantaneous (which would conform to classic distance sampling assumptions) then this probability is (more or less) equal to the proportion of time that gibbons spend calling (assuming calls are randomly distributed over the course of the day). If you are working on a period basis, you would have to calculate/estimate the probability of calling within that period.
>
> Hope that makes sense!
>
> Mark
>
>
> On Fri, 11 Sep 2020 at 10:59, Toby Pilkington <1904...@brookes.ac.uk> wrote:
> > Hi Eric,
> >
> > I have some further questions regarding the method of analysing gibbon data using the Distance R package.
> >
> > 1. I'm comparing estimates produced by triangulation, Acoustic Spatial Capture-recapture (ASCR) and Distance. I asked Ben Stevenson, the person who created the ASCR R package, about whether I can compare estimates produced by using cue rate with those produced by ASCR. He said that the calling probability in one day is a just saying that we expect 70% of groups to call in one day, it says nothing about how often they are calling. Therefore, it is not possible to convert from the probability of calls to calls emitted per hour as they are different things. I am adjusting the ASCR result using the calling probability in one day, therefore, I guess I need to take the other approach (i.e. fixing g0 to equal the calling probability in one day, e.g. 0.7) even though it's more unorthodox.
> >
> > 2. The paper I mentioned before measured the distance from each listening post in an array to each group detected for each of the four survey days. They said that if you only measure from a central point of listening posts to the central point of a detected group "the smallest distances recorded might be missed due to the “location averaging step” and lead to the violation of the assumption of perfect detection near the listening posts (g(0) = 1)". They, therefore, took this approach: "We measured
> > the distance from a listening post to the locations of a gibbon group every day and divulged the “effort” for repeated surveys in a Distance data file. In our case, if a gibbon group was detected from a listening post on n > 1 days, there would be n observations used in the analysis. Similarly, if a gibbon group was detected from m> 1 listening posts in the same day, there would be m observations used in the analysis. This did not bias the estimate of gibbon group density because m listening posts were declared in the data file. As we treated each day as one survey effort, the detection probability near the listening post was <1.0 because gibbons do not call every day. Therefore, we set the detection probability near the listening post g(0) to equal gibbon calling probability."
> >
> > I think that they considered each one of the three posts in an array as a point transect rather than the whole array (the central point of the three listening posts) to be the point transect.
> >
> >  Do you have any thoughts on this approach? I know that you are not a gibbon expert, but I just wanted to ask your thoughts on this from a Distance Sampling expert perspective.
> >
> > Many thanks,
> > Toby
> >
> > On Friday, 4 September 2020 at 18:25:26 UTC+1 Eric Rexstad wrote:
> > >
> > > Toby
> > >
> > > I can't argue with the authors of the papers you cite, but I can't think of a rational justification for using a "call probability" as an approximation for g(0).
> > > On 04/09/2020 09:32, Toby Pilkington wrote:
> > > > Hi Eric,
> > > >
> > > > Sorry, I have one further question:
> > > >
> > > > The paper I mentioned previously (Vu et al. 2018) and another paper by those authors calculated gibbon density in Distance using a slightly different method. They suggested that the assumption that g0 =1 will not be met as by using the average location of groups, the smallest distances near the listening post may be missed due to location average stepping. Furthermore, they suggest that as gibbons do not sing every day,  the assumption of g0=1 at the point can not be assumed to be true for all four survey days. They addressed this problem by doing a point transect analysis and setting g0 to equal the calling probability in one day (which for my case would be 0.7) to adjust the density estimate. What are your thoughts on this? Do you think this is a good approach or is it better to follow the cue count method and adjust the estimate using the cue rate?
> > > >
> > > > Many thanks,
> > > > Toby
> > > >
> > > > On Friday, 4 September 2020 at 09:23:37 UTC+1 Toby Pilkington wrote:
> > > > > Ahh, that makes sense. Sorry, I'm new to Distance Sampling. Thanks for clearing that up.
> > > > >
> > > > > Okay. All surveyors were trained in distance estimation, so I think it's fairly safe to assume that all the detections were measured accurately.
> > > > >
> > > > > Thanks again for your help.
> > > > >
> > > > > Cheers,
> > > > >
> > > > > On Thursday, 3 September 2020 at 14:57:34 UTC+1 Eric Rexstad wrote:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Toby
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The "area" you should specify is the size of your pristine forest to which you wish to make inference; it is nothing to do with the listening areas of each array.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Regarding your two detections, the question you have to answer is what distance you associate with those detections.  The hope would be that the distances are measured accurately.
> > > > > > On 03/09/2020 14:30, Toby Pilkington wrote:
> > > > > > > Thanks again for the quick reply and your thoughts, Eric.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > What you mentioned about the cue rates makes sense. I will try and figure out another way of calculating calling probability in one day so that I can generate a standard error.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I have a couple of quick questions:
> > > > > > > I just did a test run of the cue count analysis using the data from two of the six arrays in my data. When I tried to run the ds function, I got an error message stating that the region areas are not consistent. This is true, as the two arrays I inputted in my csv file have different values in the area column because they have different estimates of effective listening areas that I have estimated in GIS. Each array that I am analysing has a different estimated effective listening area. How do I get around this error and analyse all the data from all six arrays together?
> > > > > > > If I included two detections that I have grouped together based on their call times and proximity to each other but which the bearings do not triangulate, would that violate some of the Distance Sampling assumptions (e.g. measurements are exact)?
> > > > > > > Many thanks,
> > > > > > > Toby
> > > > > > > On Thursday, 3 September 2020 at 13:52:53 UTC+1 Eric Rexstad wrote:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Toby
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Further thoughts, my bullets correspond to your bullets--
> > > > > > > > Hopefully you can convert the call probability of 0.7 in a day into a rate.  Would it make sense that there were 0.7 calls in 4 hours of listening?  That could be converted to an hourly call rate of 0.175 calls per hour, eh?  You would need to adjust your measure of precision as well.
> > > > > > > > Yes, the value required does need to be a standard error, not a variance.
> > > > > > > > Effective detection radius is maximum listening distance divided by detection probability (provided in `ds()` output).
> > > > > > > > `ds()` cannot incorporate uncertainty in bearings in the analysis
> > > > > > > > I think you are describing the potential of making detections outside your "study area", in this case your pristine habitat type.  You could impose more stringent truncation of your radial distances (eliminating the most distant detections); this would be another way to solve this problem.
> > > > > > > > On 03/09/2020 12:43, Toby Pilkington wrote:
> > > > > > > > > Hi Eric,
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Thanks very much for the quick reply and the detailed answers. I've worked through the cue count survey vignette, which was incredibly helpful. However, I still have some questions regarding the specifics of my data analysis that maybe you can help me with:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > In the vignette, it states that for cue count you need to specify search time rather than effort. For my data, each array was surveyed for four days (each day between the hours of an average of 4 am - 8 am) and the cue rate I'm using is calling probability on one day (the probability that gibbons will call on one day). In the guidance, it states that the unit of search time and the unit of the cue rate have to be the same. The cue rate is based one day, so should I do 24 hours for the cue rate and 4 hours for search time? Or should I say that the cue rate was one day and the search time was 4 days? Or does it not matter as either option gives a search time of 4? Additionally, do you need to tell the package what units both cue rate and search time is in e.g. days or hours?
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > For the cue.rate.se <http://cue.rate.se> command, does the value have to be the standard error? As I mentioned previously, the method I am using to calculate calling probability in one day gives the variance not standard error. Could I use this variance value instead of standard error for the cue.rate.se <http://cue.rate.se>?
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > If I want to estimate the effective detection radius in the R package using a maximum listening distance of 1000 m, how would I do that? I calculated an Effective Listening Area of each array for the Triangulation analysis, which I have input into the area column in my input csv for the R package, but I've seen some papers that calculate Effective Detection Radius in Distance and I was unsure whether this would be more accurate.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Do you think I should I only include groups which bearing estimates triangulate? In addition to Distance Sampling, I’m also analysing the survey data using acoustic spatial capture-recapture (ASCR). That does not require for bearing estimates to triangulate as it factors in bearing error. Can Distance do a similar thing?
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > ·Some of the arrays are within a few hundred meters away from a different stratum that I do not want to estimate the density for (in my case I only want to estimate the density in the pristine forest area but there are two other strata in the study site: once-burnt and twice-burnt). For the triangulation analysis, I used ArcMap clip each array ELA to the pristine forest polygon to ensure that none of the ELA included burnt forest. I then only included triangulated points that fell within the ELA. Should I do the same for distance? Or would the omission of data lead to bias? Would a better option be to input a raster which is classified as pristine forest = 1, once-burnt/twice burnt = 0, so that I can tell the software the extent of the pristine forest and which points fall outside it?
> > > > > > > > > Many thanks,
> > > > > > > > > Toby
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > On Wednesday, 2 September 2020 at 13:40:41 UTC+1 Eric Rexstad wrote:
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Toby
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > I don't claim to be an expert in analysis of gibbon acoustic detection data, but here are my thoughts on your questions.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > 1. My understanding is that an array will give rise to a single detection distance, measured from the centre of the array.  The reason for the multiple listening posts is to perform the triangulation to determine the location of the vocalisation.  With that location determined, the distance from the vocalisation to the centre of the array is the radial distance that will be analysed.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > 2. Each detection by an array is a single detection, not three records for a group detection.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > 3. I presume you wish to make inference to the forest stratum in which the arrays were located.  Therefore information from all arrays are analysed together.  Effective sampling area is computed across all arrays.  The exception would be if there were array-specific covariates involved in the analysis.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > 4. No
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > 5. The estimated calling rate and its precision are called "multipliers".  Have a look at the vignette regarding cue count surveys (your gibbon survey) at our Examples website (http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-cues/cuecounts-distill.html).  In the section about `dht2` you will see how to create a named list "mult" that contains the call rate and its standard error.  The list "mult" is passed as the argument "multipliers" to the `dht2` function.  This converts density of calls to density of groups.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Hope that answers some of your questions.

messages.body_plain:
Sorry – if you have 3 listening posts, then the effort would be one for each post (point), so a total of 3 for the array.  The points will not be independent, so to get around this, you could pool the distances from each point within an array, and record effort as 3.  Or you could record each point separately with an effort of 1, and use say the bootstrap to resample the arrays of 3 points.  First method is simpler and just as good!

Steve

For the cue count method, you can ignore these issues, but you then need to estimate the number of calling events per hour say, or number of calling events per 4-hr period.  (8-11am is 3 hrs?)  This estimate needs to be an average across all groups, not just those that call on a given day.

For the point transect method, you can take g(0) as 0.7 if only 70% call on average in a 4-hr period, or you can adjust your estimate at the end for those not calling.  The two approaches should be identical.

Steve

This is because whether a gibbon calls during any time in the day is far less relevant then whether it calls whenever it is at 0 distance. Imagine that an individual gibbon (or group) calls every day (so probability of calling per day is 1), but only calls for 10% of the time while at 0 distance. This would make probability of detection at 0 distance 10%.
>
>
>
> What I think you need is the probability that a gibbon (or group) calls during each period/snapshot that you work out a density for. If your snapshots are more or less instantaneous (which would conform to classic distance sampling assumptions) then this probability is (more or less) equal to the proportion of time that gibbons spend calling (assuming calls are randomly distributed over the course of the day). If you are working on a period basis, you would have to calculate/estimate the probability of calling within that period.
>
>
>
> Hope that makes sense!

Hi Steve,

Apologies, I meant 3 hours.

Thanks very much for the suggestion. I think I'll take the point transect method. Okay, it's good to know that the two approaches should produce the same result.

Thanks,
Toby

On Friday, 11 September 2020 at 12:08:12 UTC+1 Stephen Buckland wrote:
>
> For the cue count method, you can ignore these issues, but you then need to estimate the number of calling events per hour say, or number of calling events per 4-hr period.  (8-11am is 3 hrs?)  This estimate needs to be an average across all groups, not just those that call on a given day.
>
>
>
> For the point transect method, you can take g(0) as 0.7 if only 70% call on average in a 4-hr period, or you can adjust your estimate at the end for those not calling.  The two approaches should be identical.
>

> Steve

The calling probability I have estimated is based on data collected within these four hours, not really one day, just one survey day. I guess that means it's the period method? I'm sorry, I'm not familiar with all the terminology. This calling probability I am using is generated from a gibbon density Excel package that uses the survey data to estimate it. I am using the calling probability in one day produced by this package for both the triangulation analysis and the ASCR, so I think I need to use the same one for distance.
>
>
>
> Also, regarding the g(0), I don't really understand why the researchers set g(0) to equal the calling probability. Surely in the field, a gibbon would be detected if it was singing above the point transect that you were based at.
>
>
> So, would it be correct to run the analysis using g(0) =1 and then adjust the density estimate produced by the calling probability in one day using the dht2 function?
>
>
>

> Toby

> > If I understand you correctly, I think you have a problem if you set g(0) to equal the probability of an individual gibbon (or gibbon group) calling per day. This is because whether a gibbon calls during any time in the day is far less relevant then whether it calls whenever it is at 0 distance. Imagine that an individual gibbon (or group) calls every day (so probability of calling per day is 1), but only calls for 10% of the time while at 0 distance. This would make probability of detection at 0 distance 10%.
> >
> >
> >
> > What I think you need is the probability that a gibbon (or group) calls during each period/snapshot that you work out a density for. If your snapshots are more or less instantaneous (which would conform to classic distance sampling assumptions) then this probability is (more or less) equal to the proportion of time that gibbons spend calling (assuming calls are randomly distributed over the course of the day). If you are working on a period basis, you would have to calculate/estimate the probability of calling within that period.
> >
> >
> >
> > Hope that makes sense!
> >
> >
> >
> > Mark
> >

He said that the calling probability in one day is a just saying that we expect 70% of groups to call in one day, it says nothing about how often they are calling. Therefore, it is not possible to convert from the probability of calls to calls emitted per hour as they are different things. I am adjusting the ASCR result using the calling probability in one day, therefore, I guess I need to take the other approach (i.e. fixing g0 to equal the calling probability in one day, e.g. 0.7) even though it's more unorthodox.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > 2. The paper I mentioned before measured the distance from each listening post in an array to each group detected for each of the four survey days. They said that if you only measure from a central point of listening posts to the central point of a detected group "the smallest distances recorded might be missed due to the “location averaging step” and lead to the violation of the assumption of perfect detection near the listening posts (g(0) = 1)". They, therefore, took this approach: "We measured
> > >

messages.body_plain:
Hello to all,

I wish to run DSM analyses on several bird species. However, I have a high percentage of zeros in my data, and I get the following warning when I try to run the dsm function:

Warning message: In newton(lsp = lsp, X = G$X, y = G$y, Eb = G$Eb, UrS = G$UrS, L = G$L, :   Fitting terminated with step failure - check results carefully

1. My first question is : what can be done about this warning? I have seen contrasted  opinions on this warning online, and I would like to know whether the models leading to this warning could be considered, after checking model plots, or should they be discarded based on this warning?

2. Then, when I look at the summary from my models containing a double smoothed effect of coordinates X and Y (even those WITHOUT the previous warning message I mentioned), I am very surprised to see that the p-value is not significant, and yet, the deviance explained is really high! This makes me doubt the model is valid. I have several outliers in my dataset, which I cannot delete because they were correctly sampled, and I suspect they may be responsible for this weird result. Do you have any opinions on this?

Family: Negative Binomial(0)
Link function: log Formula: Nhat ~ s(x, y, k = 10) + offset(off.set)
Parametric coefficients:
                    Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept) -23.57        20.96       -1.125    0.261

Approximate significance of smooth terms:
            edf Ref.df Chi.sq p-value
s(x,y)    2       2 1.      19       0.551
R-sq.(adj) = -215 Deviance explained = 71.3% -REML = 16.093 Scale est. = 1 n = 893

3. Lastly, I know that Hurdle models can be used to handle a high proportion of zeros in data, but I did not find any example of the use of Hurdle models in dsm, except for a project led by Filippo Franchini to build a new package integrating Hurdle models. Could you tell me if there are any other ways that I may have missed? Or alternatively, what can be done in case of a zero inflation, as I also saw that integrating ziplss into dsm models is rather complicated from a previous post (https://groups.google.com/g/distance-sampling/c/oj1j8mSmnTc/m/sg9NC4PAhDwJ)?

Many thanks for your help, and I wish you all a very nice day,

Delphine

messages.body_plain:
Hi Delphine, hi listfolk,

Thanks for providing the summary() result, this makes things easier to
diagnose, though I don't want to claim this is the real answer without
poring over the resulting model, I think it is fair to say you shouldn't
use the results provided by this model. There are a number of red flags
here as well as the warning message:

- The negative binomial parameter is estimated as 0. From the ?mgcv::nb
manual page, we know that the variance of this model is estimated as
var(y) = mu + mu^2/theta, where mu is the model mean and theta is the
parameter you estimate as 0. So we have a model with infinite variance
here (mu + mu/0 = mu + Inf = Inf), that's certainly a warning sign that
something has gone wrong.

- Your spatial smooth has only 2 estimated degrees of freedom. This most
likely means that the model form is incorrect (abundance doesn't vary in
space or k is too small, maybe?).

- The R^2 is a large negative number. Though R^2 is generally not that
useful (and you shouldn't perform model selection using it), having it
be large and negative is a sign something has gone wrong.

So to your first question: yes discard this model.

As to what to do about it: it's somewhat hard to diagnose from a
distance (please feel free to send me code/data off-list if that would
be helpful, but before you do...) It's worth checking to see if there is
some issue with your data setup, a significant amount of times these
issues are down to some problem in the setup of the tables etc rather
than a "true" issue with the data collected. The model object you have
will have a $data element. Inspecting this (specifically the Nhat and
Sample.Label columns) will let you check whether you have an issue with
how dsm is interpreting the data you gave it. Another potential issue
might be that the offset is being calculated in the incorrect units.

On hurdle-type models, I've not spend any additional time thinking about
this since the last post on this topic. The implementation is relatively
fiddly and I'm sure of the situations in which it's useful (vs Tweedie
or negbin). It probably requires some serious thought as to how this
meshes with the distance sampling part of the model.

Hope this helps.
--dave

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

 I am working with line transect data using the r package 'distance', where I am using perpendicular distances to clusters of animals. I am running into some issues as my 'N in covered region' is far larger than my density and abundance estimates and the model is telling me that the area my survey has covered in larger than my study area. I believe that this may be as a result of me using one sided transects. I am aware that using one-sided transects are not ideal for distance sampling, but is the only way that surveying is possible, as these data are being collected from a vehicle along a runway meaning that a full 360 view isn't possible. Is there a way to address this issue within the r package- i.e. tell it that each transect is only half the sampling effort when fitting the detection function? I currently have the sampling effort set to transect length- I have tried setting the effort to '0.5' but this does not seem to address the issue either. Is there something that I missing?

Would greatly appreciate any help,

Thanks,
Sam

Sam

Thanks for acknowledging the challenges of one-sided transects.

Directly to your issue, use the function `dht2` in the Distance package.  It has an argument `sample_fraction` that does exactly what you want it to do.

There is an example of the use of `sample_fraction` in the new vignette we just posted for analysis of camera trapping data in a distance sampling context.  Of course cameras are a form of point transects, while you are doing line transects, but the concept is the same.  Have a look in the section labelled "Density estimates"

http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-cameratraps/camera-distill.html#density-estimates

Hi all,

I ran some analysis on my data. However, I am not sure whether I did it correctly. The estimated covered area is larger than my survey area. I think this is because I set the effort for at four for each detection in at each array. To explain my data again, we conducted gibbon point transect surveys at six arrays, each consisting of three listening posts. Each array was surveyed for a total of four days. For the analysis, I measured the distance from each detection of a gibbon group from each listening post in the array which detected it. Because of this, I set the effort for four for all the detections in the data set. However, maybe I should have pooled the data for each array and then given an effort of four? As I am getting an effort of 72 rather than 24. However, I'm not sure how to do this in the R package. The goodness of fit for the models I ran was not good (p = 0.02), would adjusting the effort improve this? Or would it be better to go back and measure the distance from the centre of each array to the centre of each group? Or would that not change much? The survey conducted violated some of the assumptions (survey sites were located randomly to allow a comparison between a previous survey and distances estimates were not exact). Is there any way to analyse this data and make inferences?

I've attached an image of the histogram of my data if that helps.

Thanks,
Toby

messages.body_plain:
Sam,

In addition to Eric's response: I notice you said "these data are being
collected from a vehicle along a runway".  I'm not sure exactly what
this means, but if you don't have random transect locations, then you
have issues to consider in addition to that of one-sided transects.
When transects not placed at random locations within the study area, then:

(a) the density on the transects is not necessarily representative of
that in the study area, so standard ("design-based") distance sampling
methods should not be used.  Instead model-based methods (e.g., the DSM
engine) are needed to scale up from what's observed on the transects to
the study area.  It may be that you are only interested in
density/abundance on the transects, so this is not an issue.

(b) the estimated detection function may be incorrect, and hence
estimates of density on the transect may be wrong.  This occurs if there
is a density gradient in animals with respect to perpendicular distance
within the surveyed transects.  For example, if the transects are on a
road and you are interested just in density on and close to the road, it
may be that there are almost no animals actually on the road, but then
increasing density for a few hundred meters as you go away from the
road.  This means the pattern of detected distances does not tell you
about detectability alone - but is a mix of declining detectability and
increasing density.  There are methods to deal with this (e.g., Marques
et al. 2010. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1541-0420.2009.01381.x ; also a
Mark recapture distance sampling) but they require special data
collection protocols.  Another option is to do a set of transect
perpendicular to the roads to check how density varies in that direction
(and hopefully show it does not!).

You can find more discussion of these issues in previous postings to
this group (search for, e.g., "Roadside").

I hope this is helpful!

Len

--

Toby

I'll remain silent on the subject of how effort should be defined for your survey, you and Prof Buckland have been chasing around that idea.

However, I can comment upon your histogram.  As these are point count surveys, have you used the 'transect="point"' argument in the 'ds()' function?  If you didn't (and used the default 'transect="line"') that may have something to do with your fit statistic.  Adjusting effort will not alter the fit of your model to your data.

Because of this, I set the effort for four for all the detections in the data set. However, maybe I should have pooled the data for each array and then given an effort of four? As I am getting an effort of 72 rather than 24. However, I'm not sure how to do this in the R package. Or would it be better to go back and measure the distance from the centre of each array to the centre of each group? Or would that not change much? The survey conducted violated some of the assumptions (survey sites were located randomly to allow a comparison between a previous survey and distances estimates were not exact). messages.body_plain:
Hi Toby,

I've attached a graph of what I think your plot of detection density versus distance should look like. If you group the distance bands astutely I reckon you should have no problems fitting a detection function quite neatly to these data. However, given the fact that your distances should be quite precise (if your triangulation method is working well) it seems a little odd to me that you have such marked jumps in density - particularly between 300-400 and 400-500m, and between 800-900m and 900-1000m. I would often expect these to be associated with rounding or 'clumped estimates' such as you often get where distances are estimated by observers. But if I understood your data correctly, that shouldn't be happening here, so it might be indicating that something else (I don't know what) is going on with your data. Might be worth getting the views of other folk on this forum with greater experience of a wider range of distance sampling surveys.

Cheers,

Mark

This is because whether a gibbon calls during any time in the day is far less relevant then whether it calls whenever it is at 0 distance. Imagine that an individual gibbon (or group) calls every day (so probability of calling per day is 1), but only calls for 10% of the time while at 0 distance. > > > >

If you didn't (and used the default 'transect="line"') that may have something to do with your fit statistic.  Adjusting effort will not alter the fit of your model to your data.

I think this is because I set the effort for at four for each detection in at each array. To explain my data again, we conducted gibbon point transect surveys at six arrays, each consisting of three listening posts. Each array was surveyed for a total of four days. For the analysis, I measured the distance from each detection of a gibbon group from each listening post in the array which detected it. Because of this, I set the effort for four for all the detections in the data set. However, maybe I should have pooled the data for each array and then given an effort of four? As I am getting an effort of 72 rather than 24. However, I'm not sure how to do this in the R package. The goodness of fit for the models I ran was not good (p = 0.02), would adjusting the effort improve this? Or would it be better to go back and measure the distance from the centre of each array to the centre of each group? Or would that not change much? The survey conducted violated some of the assumptions (survey sites were located randomly to allow a comparison between a previous survey and distances estimates were not exact). Is there any way to analyse this data and make inferences?

> > > > >
> > > > > Hi Toby,
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > If I understand you correctly, I think you have a problem if you set g(0) to equal the probability of an individual gibbon (or gibbon group) calling per day. This is because whether a gibbon calls during any time in the day is far less relevant then whether it calls whenever it is at 0 distance. Imagine that an individual gibbon (or group) calls every day (so probability of calling per day is 1), but only calls for 10% of the time while at 0 distance. This would make probability of detection at 0 distance 10%.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > What I think you need is the probability that a gibbon (or group) calls during each period/snapshot that you work out a density for. If your snapshots are more or less instantaneous (which would conform to classic distance sampling assumptions) then this probability is (more or less) equal to the proportion of time that gibbons spend calling (assuming calls are randomly distributed over the course of the day). If you are working on a period basis, you would have to calculate/estimate the probability of calling within that period.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Hope that makes sense!

> > > > > >

> > > > > > 1. I'm comparing estimates produced by triangulation, Acoustic Spatial Capture-recapture (ASCR) and Distance. I asked Ben Stevenson, the person who created the ASCR R package, about whether I can compare estimates produced by using cue rate with those produced by ASCR. He said that the calling probability in one day is a just saying that we expect 70% of groups to call in one day, it says nothing about how often they are calling. Therefore, it is not possible to convert from the probability of calls to calls emitted per hour as they are different things. I am adjusting the ASCR result using the calling probability in one day, therefore, I guess I need to take the other approach (i.e. fixing g0 to equal the calling probability in one day, e.g. 0.7) even though it's more unorthodox.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 2. The paper I mentioned before measured the distance from each listening post in an array to each group detected for each of the four survey days. They said that if you only measure from a central point of listening posts to the central point of a detected group "the smallest distances recorded might be missed due to the “location averaging step” and lead to the violation of the assumption of perfect detection near the listening posts (g(0) = 1)". They, therefore, took this approach: "We measured
> > > > > >
> > > > > > the distance from a listening post to the locations of a gibbon group every day and divulged the “effort” for repeated surveys in a Distance data file. In our case, if a gibbon group was detected from a listening post on n > 1 days, there would be n observations used in the analysis. Similarly, if a gibbon group was detected from m> 1 listening posts in the same day, there would be m observations used in the analysis. This did not bias the estimate of gibbon group density because m listening posts were declared in the data file. As we treated each day as one survey effort, the detection probability near the listening post was <1.0 because gibbons do not call every day. Therefore, we set the detection probability near the listening post g(0) to equal gibbon calling probability."
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I think that they considered each one of the three posts in an array as a point transect rather than the whole array (the central point of the three listening posts) to be the point transect.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >  Do you have any thoughts on this approach? I know that you are not a gibbon expert, but I just wanted to ask your thoughts on this from a Distance Sampling expert perspective.

Hi Mark,

Thanks for the advice. Like I said to Eric, I think there are issues with the data. The team consisted mostly of novice gibbon surveyors, therefore I think there are many errors in bearing and distance estimates. I'll try and do what I can with the data.

On Monday, 14 September 2020 at 15:05:18 UTC+1 Mark Wilson wrote:
> Hi Toby,
>
> I've attached a graph of what I think your plot of detection density versus distance should look like. If you group the distance bands astutely I reckon you should have no problems fitting a detection function quite neatly to these data. However, given the fact that your distances should be quite precise (if your triangulation method is working well) it seems a little odd to me that you have such marked jumps in density - particularly between 300-400 and 400-500m, and between 800-900m and 900-1000m. I would often expect these to be associated with rounding or 'clumped estimates' such as you often get where distances are estimated by observers. But if I understood your data correctly, that shouldn't be happening here, so it might be indicating that something else (I don't know what) is going on with your data. Might be worth getting the views of other folk on this forum with greater experience of a wider range of distance sampling surveys.
>
> Cheers,
>
> Mark

For the analysis, I measured the distance from each detection of a gibbon group from each listening post in the array which detected it. Because of this, I set the effort for four for all the detections in the data set. However, maybe I should have pooled the data for each array and then given an effort of four? As I am getting an effort of 72 rather than 24. However, I'm not sure how to do this in the R package. The goodness of fit for the models I ran was not good (p = 0.02), would adjusting the effort improve this? Or would it be better to go back and measure the distance from the centre of each array to the centre of each group? Or would that not change much? The survey conducted violated some of the assumptions (survey sites were located randomly to allow a comparison between a previous survey and distances estimates were not exact). Is there any way to analyse this data and make inferences?

> > > > > If I understand you correctly, I think you have a problem if you set g(0) to equal the probability of an individual gibbon (or gibbon group) calling per day. This is because whether a gibbon calls during any time in the day is far less relevant then whether it calls whenever it is at 0 distance. Imagine that an individual gibbon (or group) calls every day (so probability of calling per day is 1), but only calls for 10% of the time while at 0 distance. This would make probability of detection at 0 distance 10%.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > What I think you need is the probability that a gibbon (or group) calls during each period/snapshot that you work out a density for. If your snapshots are more or less instantaneous (which would conform to classic distance sampling assumptions) then this probability is (more or less) equal to the proportion of time that gibbons spend calling (assuming calls are randomly distributed over the course of the day). If you are working on a period basis, you would have to calculate/estimate the probability of calling within that period.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > 3. I presume you wish to make inference to the forest stratum in which the arrays were located.  Therefore information from all arrays are analysed together. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 4. No
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > 5. The estimated calling rate and its precision are called "multipliers".  Have a look at the vignette regarding cue count surveys (your gibbon survey) at our Examples website (http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-cues/cuecounts-distill.html).  In the section about `dht2` you will see how to create a named list "mult" that contains the call rate and its standard error.  The list "mult" is passed as the argument "multipliers" to the `dht2` function.  This converts density of calls to density of groups.

Angela

Setting aside AIC rank for the moment, making inference based upon a model that does not fit your observed data does not result in defensible estimates.  Your estimates will be open to criticism that you've used a model that is in conflict with the data you observed.

More reliable estimates are derived from employing models that fit your distance sampling data.

messages.body_plain:
Just to come back to this. Delphine and I corresponded off-list and I
had a look at her data. The issue was that the Sample.Labels did not
match for the bulk of the observations. This lead to only 2 non-zero
segment counts.

You can check this by looking at model$data$count or
model$data$abundance.est to see what the computed response values are.

I'll look at putting-in some better checks in the future so dsm can warn
you if this happens.

best,
--dave

On 14/09/2020 10:08, David Lawrence Miller wrote:
> Hi Delphine, hi listfolk,
>
> Thanks for providing the summary() result, this makes things easier to
> diagnose, though I don't want to claim this is the real answer without
> poring over the resulting model, I think it is fair to say you shouldn't
> use the results provided by this model. There are a number of red flags
> here as well as the warning message:
>
> - The negative binomial parameter is estimated as 0. From the ?mgcv::nb
> manual page, we know that the variance of this model is estimated as
> var(y) = mu + mu^2/theta, where mu is the model mean and theta is the
> parameter you estimate as 0. So we have a model with infinite variance
> here (mu + mu/0 = mu + Inf = Inf), that's certainly a warning sign that
> something has gone wrong.
>
> - Your spatial smooth has only 2 estimated degrees of freedom. This most
> likely means that the model form is incorrect (abundance doesn't vary in
> space or k is too small, maybe?).
>
> - The R^2 is a large negative number. Though R^2 is generally not that
> useful (and you shouldn't perform model selection using it), having it
> be large and negative is a sign something has gone wrong.
>
> So to your first question: yes discard this model.
>
> As to what to do about it: it's somewhat hard to diagnose from a
> distance (please feel free to send me code/data off-list if that would
> be helpful, but before you do...) It's worth checking to see if there is
> some issue with your data setup, a significant amount of times these
> issues are down to some problem in the setup of the tables etc rather
> than a "true" issue with the data collected. The model object you have
> will have a $data element. Inspecting this (specifically the Nhat and
> Sample.Label columns) will let you check whether you have an issue with
> how dsm is interpreting the data you gave it. Another potential issue
> might be that the offset is being calculated in the incorrect units.
>
> On hurdle-type models, I've not spend any additional time thinking about
> this since the last post on this topic. The implementation is relatively
> fiddly and I'm sure of the situations in which it's useful (vs Tweedie
> or negbin). It probably requires some serious thought as to how this
> meshes with the distance sampling part of the model.
>
>
> Hope this helps.
> --dave
>
> On 14/09/2020 07:21, ducros....@gmail.com wrote:

>> high percentage of zeros in my data, and I get the following warning

>>

>> = G$UrS, L = G$L, : Fitting terminated with step failure - check
>> results carefully
>>
>> 1. My first question is : what can be done about this warning? I have

>>
>> 2. Then, when I look at the summary from my models containing a double
>> smoothed effect of coordinates X and Y (even those WITHOUT the
>> previous warning message I mentioned), I am very surprised to see that
>> the p-value is not significant, and yet, the deviance explained is
>> really high! This makes me doubt the model is valid. I have several
>> outliers in my dataset, which I cannot delete because they were

>> weird result. Do you have any opinions on this?

>> Family: Negative Binomial(0)

messages.subject: R-Distance giving wrong abundance estimate?
messages.subject_clean: R-Distance giving wrong abundance estimate?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I talked with Steve Buckland and he suggested Ipost my problem in the group.

I´ve done some abundance estimates of bluefin tuna in the Mediterranean with Distance in R. In the example I comment on in this mail, I modela detection function for 3 years (2010-2011-2013) and then derive abundance estimates for each year separately.

As you see in the table below (extracted directly from R), the abundance of clusters for area A is given as 10 in the model summary, but it should be  61837*8/(2.67917*6093) = 30.30, and I can´t figure out why.

The final model is obtained with this line (I attach the object of the final model, and the summary) :

final.model<-ds(obs.table, truncation=list(right=trunc, left=left), adjustment=NULL, key=key.name <http://key.name/>, formula=as.formula(paste0("~", covar3.1,"+",covar3.2,"+",covar3.3)))

I see something wrong in the summary model, which is done for the whole dataset including the three years 2010-2011-2013 as it is not getting the right Effort.  When I check the sample.table, the total effort for Region "A" is 20578 km, but the summary table shows 2177 km....and I don´t know where this comes from (when extracting the Nat for 2010, the Effort is correct, 6093km for Region A in 2010).

To extract the estimate for 2010 I use:

Nhat_2010 <- dht(final.model$ddf, region.table.est, sample.table.2010,obs.table.2010).

I attach the object Nhat_2010 so you can see it in R.

So, I don´t know if I did something wrong in the setup or R is doing something wrong for some reason:

- The effort in the final model is wrong

- The estimate of abundance in the 2010 filtered data is wrong (being Effort right here)...and presumably wrong for all years

Any suggestion on where the problem is?

Thanks

Ana Cañadas

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] R-Distance giving wrong abundance estimate?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ana, hi listfolk,

It's somewhat hard to tell from the files you sent (as they are model
output not the original data.frames that go into the analysis). Best I
can make out is that there is an issue with the column names in the data
you provide.

For example, looking at the data given to the detection function, there
are many columns with very similar names (e.g., "Region.Label",
"Region.Label.1"). An issue in R is that column names match on partial
completion, so you can obtain data$foobar by typing only data$foo
(provided there is no $foo element in data). I've attempted to remove
bugs caused by this issue from mrds/Distance previously but I think some
still lurk in there. Which brings me to one potential issue you may have...

The model data seems to have a column called Effort.original but no
column called Effort. It's possible this column may be causing the
issue. I recommend re-formatting your data, with a minimal number of
columns and avoiding column names that have the potential for this
partial matching collision and see if this solves your issue.

I'll look into this issue in mrds/Distance and see if we have some
remaining places where this issue can crop up and try to patch these for
the next release.

Hope this helps.

cheers,
--dave

messages.subject: Live distance sampling training workshop, online from Univ St Andrews, 09-20 November 2020. Registration Open.
messages.subject_clean: Live distance sampling training workshop, online from Univ St Andrews, 09-20 November 2020. Registration Open.
messages.body_plain:
Interactive introductory distance sampling training

The University of St Andrews has been training people in design and analysis of distance sampling studies for decades.  Perhaps you've wanted to attend but could not get permission for travel to Scotland or the scheduling of workshops conflicted with your field work. 👨‍🌾

We are offering the training workshop in 10 two-hour blocks in November 🍂.  You will be invited to interact in short lectures on distance sampling principles. 👩‍🎓 Exercises analysing data sets in R will reinforce those principles and the lecturer will be available to assist during the practical session via screen sharing.  The block will conclude with a summary of the exercise and question/answer session for both lecture and exercise. 💻  You can participate in polls during the workshop to assess your comprehension of topics discussed. 🤔

The workshop will be delivered using Zoom web conferencing software along with R-Studio "in the cloud".☁️ You will need (free) accounts for both pieces of software. I encourage you to experiment with Zoom (at https://zoom.us) and https://rstudio.cloud before the course begins. 👩‍💻  There will be an internet connection testing session prior to the first meeting on 09 November.

Companion online training workshops

We are planning an additional advanced distance sampling workshops in January and March 2021.  These workshops will require knowledge of basic distance sampling principles derived from this introductory training workshop.

Important details

    Workshop dates and time: 09-20 November 2020, 1500-1700 Greenwich Mean Time. For the time of day in your zone, follow this link <https://www.timeanddate.com/worldclock/fixedtime.html?p1=3853&iso=20201109T15&msg=Introductory%20distance%20sampling%20training%20workshop%20from%20St%20Andrews&ah=2>.  🕰️
    Registration deadline: 23 October 2020📅
    Enrolment limit: 15
    Cost: 215 British pounds 💵
    What is included: Lectures, exercises, code, data all available online📃

What they are saying

I would like to say I really liked RStudio Cloud and it is working just fine and I am really enjoying using it as a student. I'm looking forward to using it as an instructor too. I really liked the first half of the course. I love distance sampling and I am enjoying every second of the course! The only thing I can say about this particular workshop is it deserves more time. -- Kaan Özgencil, PhD student, Department of Biological Sciences, Middle East Technical University, Ankara

Further details are available at:

http://workshops.distancesampling.org/intro-nov-2020.html

At this page you will find a link to the St Andrews online shop where payment is made.  After payment is made, I will contact you with additional details regarding workshop electronic materials, etc. Feel free to contact me with questions.

Information regarding all distance sampling workshops can be found at

https://workshops.distancesampling.org
--
Eric Rexstad
Centre for Ecological and Environmental Modelling
University of St Andrews
St Andrews is a charity registered in Scotland SC013532
